title: Inequalities, Lp spaces, and modes of convergence

sections.title: Markov inequality and a zero-integral consequence
paragraphs: The lecture begins with inequalities and convergence, recalling $\mathbb E X=\int_\Omega X(\omega)\,\mathbb P(d\omega)$. On any measure space, if $f\ge0$ is measurable, then for every $t>0$, $$t\,\mu(\{f\ge t\})\le\mu(f).$$
proof: Take the simple function $\varphi=t\mathbf1_{\{f\ge t\}}\le f$ and use monotonicity: $$t\,\mu(\{f\ge t\})=\mu_0(\varphi)\le\mu(f).$$

Consequently, if $f\ge0$ and $\mu(f)=0$, then $f=0$ almost everywhere. Indeed, for $A_n=\{f\ge1/n\}$, Markov gives $\mu(A_n)\le n\mu(f)=0$. Since $A_n\uparrow A_\infty=\{f>0\}$, continuity from below yields $\mu(A_\infty)=0$.

sections.title: Transformed Markov bounds: Chebyshev and Chernoff
paragraphs: Let $X$ be a real-valued random variable and let $\psi:\mathbb R\to[0,\infty]$ be Borel measurable. For $A\in\mathcal B_{\mathbb R}$, define $$\psi_*(A)=\inf\{\psi(x):x\in A\}.$$ Then $$\psi_*(A)\mathbb P(X\in A)\le\mathbb E\psi(X).$$ Apply Markov to the measurable nonnegative function $\omega\mapsto\psi(X(\omega))$, or directly use $\psi_*(A)\mathbf1_{\{X\in A\}}\le\psi(X)$.

Taking $\psi(x)=x_+$ gives, for $t>0$, $$\mathbb P(X\ge t)\le t^{-1}\mathbb E X_+.$$ Taking $\psi(x)=|x-\mathbb E X|^2$ for $X\in L^2$ gives Chebyshev: $$\mathbb P(|X-\mathbb E X|\ge t)\le t^{-2}\operatorname{Var}(X),\qquad \operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E X)^2].$$

Taking $\psi(x)=e^{\lambda x}$ gives the Chernoff bound $$\mathbb P(X\ge t)\le e^{-\lambda t}\mathbb E e^{\lambda X},\qquad t\in\mathbb R,\ \lambda\ge0.$$ The choice $\lambda=0$ gives the trivial bound $1$; positive $\lambda$ is useful when the exponential moment is finite.
editorial: The infimum convention is $\inf\varnothing=+\infty$; nonnegative integral products use $0\cdot\infty=0$. Divide by $\psi_*(A)$ only when it is finite and strictly positive. Chebyshev is a centered two-sided bound; the displayed Chernoff version is an upper-tail bound.

sections.title: Vector Jensen inequality and supporting hyperplanes
paragraphs: Let $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open and convex, let $g:Q\to\mathbb R$ be convex, and let $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ be an integrable random vector with $\mathbb P(X\in Q)=1$. If $g(X)$ is integrable, Jensen gives $$\mathbb E g(X)\ge g(\mathbb E X).$$
proof: First show $\mu=\mathbb E X\in Q$. If $\mu\notin Q$, separation provides a vector $v\in\mathbb R^d$ and $a\in\mathbb R$ with $\langle v,x\rangle>a$ for every $x\in Q$ and $\langle v,\mu\rangle\le a$. Since $X\in Q$ almost surely, $$\mathbb E\langle v,X\rangle>a,$$ while linearity gives $\mathbb E\langle v,X\rangle=\langle v,\mu\rangle\le a$, a contradiction.

Convexity on the open convex set supplies a supporting vector $u(x_0)$ at each $x_0\in Q$ such that $$g(x)\ge g(x_0)+\langle u(x_0),x-x_0\rangle\quad(x\in Q).$$ Set $x_0=\mu$ and take expectations to get $$\mathbb E g(X)\ge g(\mu)+\langle u(\mu),\mathbb E X-\mu\rangle=g(\mu).$$
editorial: The separation theorem and existence of a supporting hyperplane are the convex-analysis inputs used in this board proof. The strict expected inequality uses the fact that a strictly positive integrable random variable has strictly positive expectation.

recall.question: How does a supporting hyperplane prove vector Jensen, and why must $\mathbb E X$ lie in the convex domain?
answer: If the mean were outside the open convex domain, a separating hyperplane would put every possible value of $X$ strictly on one side and its mean on the other, contradicting linearity of expectation. At the mean, a supporting affine function lies below $g$; its expected linear term vanishes.
checks: Keep the open convex domain and integrability hypotheses.
Evaluate the supporting affine function at the mean.
Explain which convex-analysis facts are being used.

sections.title: Moment quantities and nesting of the Lp spaces
paragraphs: For $p>0$, write $$L^p(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)=\{X:\mathbb E|X|^p<\infty\},\qquad \|X\|_p=(\mathbb E|X|^p)^{1/p}.$$ On a probability space, for $0<p<q$, $$\|X\|_p\le\|X\|_q,\qquad L^q\subseteq L^p.$$
proof: The function $g(u)=u^{q/p}$ is convex on $[0,\infty)$. Jensen applied to $|X|^p$ gives $$\mathbb E|X|^q=\mathbb E[(|X|^p)^{q/p}]\ge(\mathbb E|X|^p)^{q/p}.$$ Taking the $q$th root proves the comparison.
editorial: The bracketed inclusion on handwritten p40 is reversed: the displayed norm inequality implies $L^q\subseteq L^p$, as written here. For full generality, apply Jensen first to $\min(|X|,n)^p$, then use monotone convergence; this does not assume the lower moment is finite in advance. When $p<1$, $\|\cdot\|_p$ is a moment quantity or quasi-norm, not a norm. The total probability $1$ is needed for this comparison without a measure-mass factor.

sections.title: Hölder inequality, Young inequality, and equality
paragraphs: If $p,q>1$ satisfy $1/p+1/q=1$, then for random variables on the same probability space, $$\mathbb E|XY|\le\|X\|_p\|Y\|_q.$$ The case $p=q=2$ is Cauchy-Schwarz. No independence assumption is needed.
proof: First assume the norms are finite and nonzero, and divide $X,Y$ by their respective norms. It is enough to treat $\|X\|_p=\|Y\|_q=1$. For $x,y\ge0$, Young inequality is $$\frac{x^p}{p}+\frac{y^q}{q}\ge xy.$$ For fixed $x$, minimize $h(y)=x^p/p+y^q/q-xy$. Its derivative is $h^{\prime}(y)=y^{q-1}-x$, so the minimum occurs at $y=x^{p-1}$, where $y^q=x^p$ and $h(y)=x^p(1/p+1/q-1)=0$. The small convex graph in the notes shows this minimum.

Apply Young pointwise and take expectations: $$\mathbb E|XY|\le\mathbb E\left(\frac{|X|^p}{p}+\frac{|Y|^q}{q}\right)=\frac1p+\frac1q=1.$$ Rescaling proves Hölder. If either norm is zero, the corresponding variable is zero almost surely. Cases with infinite positive norms make the bound immediate.

With the unit-norm normalization, equality holds exactly when the nonnegative Young gap is zero almost surely. Equivalently, $$|X|=|Y|^{q-1}\quad\text{almost surely},\qquad |X|^p=|Y|^q\quad\text{almost surely}.$$
editorial: Without normalization, the equality condition for finite nonzero norms is $|X|^p/\|X\|_p^p=|Y|^q/\|Y\|_q^q$ almost surely. Absolute values are essential; Hölder bounds the absolute product. The scalar calculus proof and normalization are both part of the lecture.

sections.title: Essential supremum and Minkowski inequality
paragraphs: The essential supremum norm is $$\|X\|_\infty=\inf\{t\ge0:\mathbb P(|X|>t)=0\}.$$ It ignores changes on null events. Minkowski inequality states that for $1\le p<\infty$ and $X,Y\in L^p$, $$\|X+Y\|_p\le\|X\|_p+\|Y\|_p.$$
proof: Before dividing by a norm, establish finiteness. For $p\ge1$ and $a,b\ge0$, Jensen gives $$(a+b)^p\le2^{p-1}(a^p+b^p).$$ Hence $$\|X+Y\|_p\le2^{1-1/p}(\|X\|_p^p+\|Y\|_p^p)^{1/p}\le2^{1-1/p}(\|X\|_p+\|Y\|_p)<\infty.$$ This preliminary estimate has an extra factor; the next argument removes it.

The case $p=1$ follows directly from $|X+Y|\le|X|+|Y|$. For $p>1$ take $q=p/(p-1)$, so $(p-1)q=p$. Hölder gives $$\mathbb E|X+Y|^p\le\mathbb E[(|X|+|Y|)|X+Y|^{p-1}]\le(\|X\|_p+\|Y\|_p)(\mathbb E|X+Y|^{(p-1)q})^{1/q}=(\|X\|_p+\|Y\|_p)\|X+Y\|_p^{p-1}.$$ If the last norm is positive, divide by its $(p-1)$st power; if it is zero, the result is immediate.
editorial: Correction to p41: the annotation “works for any $p>0$” cannot apply to the displayed Jensen estimate with factor $2^{1-1/p}$. For $0<p<1$, the valid estimate is $\mathbb E|X+Y|^p\le\mathbb E|X|^p+\mathbb E|Y|^p$. Equivalently, $\|X+Y\|_p\le2^{1/p-1}(\|X\|_p+\|Y\|_p)$. Ordinary Minkowski generally fails below $1$. For example, indicators of disjoint events of probability $1/2$ have sum norm $1$, while the sum of their $p$-quantities is $2^{1-1/p}<1$. The essential supremum separately obeys the triangle inequality by the pointwise bound outside a null set.

recall.question: Where does Hölder enter the proof of Minkowski, and why is finiteness checked before division?
answer: Write $|X+Y|^p\le(|X|+|Y|)|X+Y|^{p-1}$ and apply Hölder to each summand with conjugate exponent $q=p/(p-1)$. The identity $(p-1)q=p$ produces a common factor $\|X+Y\|_p^{p-1}$. A preliminary convexity estimate makes that factor finite; then handle the zero case or divide.
checks: Do not divide by zero or infinity.
Do not extend Minkowski below p=1.

sections.title: From a seminorm on variables to a norm on equivalence classes
paragraphs: For $p\ge1$, the collection of variables with finite $p$th moment is a vector space: $X\in L^p$ implies $aX\in L^p$, and Minkowski gives $X+Y\in L^p$. The quantity $\|\cdot\|_p$ is homogeneous and satisfies the triangle inequality, but $\|X\|_p=0$ means only that $X=0$ almost surely.

Thus it is a seminorm on literal measurable functions. Define $$X\sim Y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\mathbb P(X\ne Y)=0.$$ Passing to the quotient by this equivalence makes $L^p$ a normed vector space; two representatives differing only on a null event are the same element.
editorial: The lecture uses $L^p$ for the quotient after first discussing actual variables. The usual notation often suppresses that distinction. For $0<p<1$ the quotient is still useful, but the displayed moment quantity is not a norm.

sections.title: Three convergence modes and their first implications
paragraphs: For random variables $(X_n)_{n\ge1}$ and $X_\infty$ on one probability space, almost-sure convergence means $$\mathbb P(\{\omega:\lim_nX_n(\omega)\text{ exists and equals }X_\infty(\omega)\})=1.$$ Convergence in probability, written $X_n\xrightarrow{\mathbb P}X_\infty$, means $$\mathbb P(|X_n-X_\infty|\ge\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0\quad\text{for every }\varepsilon>0.$$ For $p>0$, convergence in $L^p$ means $X_n,X_\infty\in L^p$ and $$\mathbb E|X_n-X_\infty|^p\longrightarrow0.$$
For finite real-valued limits, almost-sure convergence implies convergence in probability.
proof: For fixed $\varepsilon>0$, consider $$B_{n,\varepsilon}=\left\{\sup_{m\ge n}|X_m-X_\infty|\ge\varepsilon\right\}.$$ These tail events decrease with $n$. On a path converging to $X_\infty$, the tail supremum eventually falls below $\varepsilon$, so $\mathbb P(\bigcap_n B_{n,\varepsilon})=0$. Continuity from above gives $\mathbb P(B_{n,\varepsilon})\to0$. Since $\{|X_n-X_\infty|\ge\varepsilon\}\subseteq B_{n,\varepsilon}$, convergence in probability follows.
editorial: Using $>$ instead of $\ge$ in the definition of convergence in probability is equivalent: change the positive threshold slightly. For infinite limits use a metric on the extended real line rather than absolute subtraction.

sections.title: The sweeping-interval counterexample
paragraphs: Convergence in probability need not imply almost-sure convergence. On $((0,1],\mathcal B_{(0,1]},\text{uniform measure})$, set $$X_{k,\ell}(\omega)=\mathbf1_{[\ell/k,(\ell+1)/k]}(\omega),\qquad k\ge1,\quad0\le\ell<k.$$ Enumerate row by row: $$X_{1,0},\ X_{2,0},X_{2,1},\ X_{3,0},X_{3,1},X_{3,2},\ldots.$$ The horizontal bar in the notes shows a cell of length $1/k$ moving across the full interval.

Each row-$k$ variable has $\mathbb P(X_{k,\ell}\ne0)=1/k\to0$ as the enumeration proceeds. Thus the enumerated sequence converges to zero in probability. Yet every fixed $\omega\in(0,1]$ belongs to a cell in every row, so its path is $1$ infinitely often and does not tend to zero.
editorial: For all sufficiently large rows each fixed outcome is also outside some cells; hence each path has infinitely many zeros as well. In fact $\mathbb E|X_{k,\ell}|^p=1/k$ for every $p>0$, so this same example converges to zero in every finite $L^p$ while failing almost-sure convergence. The closed cell endpoints can overlap, but endpoints have zero uniform mass and do not change the probability calculation.

sections.title: Lp convergence, shrinking spikes, and continuous maps
paragraphs: For every $p>0$, convergence in $L^p$ implies convergence in probability: $$\mathbb P(|X_n-X_\infty|\ge\varepsilon)\le\varepsilon^{-p}\mathbb E|X_n-X_\infty|^p\longrightarrow0.$$ This is Markov applied to the powered error.

The converse fails. On the uniform interval take $$X_n(\omega)=2^n\mathbf1_{(0,1/n]}(\omega),\qquad X_\infty=0.$$ Then $\mathbb P(X_n\ne0)=1/n\to0$, and every fixed $\omega>0$ is eventually outside the shrinking interval, so convergence is also almost sure. Nevertheless, for every fixed $p>0$, $$\mathbb E|X_n-X_\infty|^p=\frac{2^{np}}{n}\longrightarrow\infty.$$ Thus this one sequence fails convergence in every finite $L^p$, despite converging almost surely and in probability to zero.

Almost-sure convergence and finite-$p$ convergence in $L^p$ have no implication in either direction in general: use the sweeping intervals for one direction and suitably growing shrinking spikes for the other. If $X_n\to0$ almost surely and $f$ is continuous at $0$, then $f(X_n)\to f(0)$ almost surely. Continuity alone does not produce convergence in $L^p$.
editorial: The handwritten spike has exponential height $2^n$ and support $(0,1/n]$. Both the height and the moment calculation are retained: for each $p>0$, exponential growth $2^{np}$ dominates the denominator $n$. Each individual term still has a finite $p$th moment.

recall.question: Give examples separating convergence almost surely, in probability, and in Lp.
answer: The sweeping-cell sequence converges in probability and in every finite $L^p$, but not almost surely. The lecture spike $2^n\mathbf1_{(0,1/n]}$ on the uniform interval converges almost surely and in probability to zero, while its $p$th moment $2^{np}/n$ diverges for every $p>0$. Markov proves that $L^p$ convergence always implies convergence in probability.
